title: Note-taking and understanding
introHtml:
Good notes are a tool for testing yourself later, not a copy of the lecture, the book or the video. Keep them short, in your own words, and built around questions.

The useful question about any note format is not "does it look complete?" but "what will I do with this page next week?" Notes you can quiz yourself from, redraw from memory or compare across topics keep paying back. Notes you can only re-read pay back very little. The time costs below use the same scale as the rest of this compendium (one recall question of about 30 seconds = 1×); they are rough estimates from typical practice, not measured values.

items.title: Cornell notes
items.leadHtml: Split the page into a narrow left column and a wide right column. Notes go on the right; afterwards, write questions on the left. Review by covering the right side and answering.

parts.why: The page layout builds the test into the notes. Writing the notes is the cheap, passive part; writing the cue questions forces you to decide what each chunk is for, and covering the right column turns every later review into retrieval practice instead of re-reading. Think of it as notes with the answer key folded behind them.
parts.how:
1. Draw a vertical line about a third of the way across the page, and leave 4-5 lines free at the bottom.
  2. During the class or reading, write brief notes in the wide right column. Skip lines between ideas.
  3. Within a day, write one question or cue word in the left column next to each chunk.
  4. At the bottom, write a two- or three-sentence summary of the page in your own words.
  5. To review, cover the right column, answer each question aloud or on scrap paper, then uncover and check.

examples.simple: A school history lesson on the causes of the First World War. Left column: "What were the four long-term causes (MAIN)?" Right column: militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism, each with one detail.
examples.nontrivial: An introductory economics lecture on elasticity. Instead of cues that only ask for definitions ("What is price elasticity?"), write cues that force use: "Why does a tax on cigarettes raise revenue but barely cut smoking?" The answer requires the definition and the idea that demand for addictive goods is inelastic, so one cue tests two layers.

  • Non-trivial: An introductory economics lecture on elasticity. Instead of cues that only ask for definitions ("What is price elasticity?"), write cues that force use: "Why does a tax on cigarettes raise revenue but barely cut smoking?" The answer requires the definition and the idea that demand for addictive goods is inelastic, so one cue tests two layers.

parts.time: About +2-4 min per paragraph's worth of notes over plain notes (~4-8×), most of it in writing the cue questions.
parts.watch: Writing the questions and never covering the right column again gives you the cost without the benefit. Cues that only name a topic ("Elasticity") are weaker than real questions.

items.title: Question-based notes
items.leadHtml: Write each heading as a question ("How does the kidney concentrate urine?", "Why did the Weimar Republic collapse?", "When should I use a hash map instead of a list?"). The notes become a quiz you made yourself.

parts.why: A statement heading ("Weimar Republic") tells you where you are; a question heading tells you what you are supposed to be able to do. While you take notes, the question acts like a filter: anything that does not help answer it is probably a detail. Later, the headings alone are a ready-made test. It is the same idea as Cornell notes with the questions moved to the top.
parts.how:
1. Before the class or chapter, turn each section title into a "how", "why" or "what happens if" question.
  2. Take notes under each question, aiming to answer it in a few lines.
  3. Add new questions when the lecturer or author raises something you did not expect.
  4. To review, read only the headings and answer each one before looking at the notes underneath.

examples.simple: A biology chapter heading "Photosynthesis" becomes "Where does the oxygen released in photosynthesis come from?"
examples.nontrivial: In a contract law course, the topic "Offer and acceptance" becomes several questions that mirror how exam problems are set: "When does an advert count as an offer?", "When is an emailed acceptance effective?", "What happens if the reply changes a term?" Each question is a small problem, so the notes double as practice for problem questions, not just for definitions.

items.title: Annotate the slides instead of rewriting them
items.leadHtml: When the lecture slides (or a handout, textbook chapter or set of lecture notes) are the spine, add your notes, links and "why" answers directly on them rather than copying them out.

parts.why: Copying out slides costs a lot of time and attention, and most of it goes into handwriting, not thinking. If the content is already on the page, your scarce attention in a lecture is better spent on what the slides leave out: the lecturer's explanation, the example, the "this is the bit people get wrong". An experiment on slide handouts found that students who had the handouts during the lecture took fewer notes but did at least as well on later tests as students who had to write more.
parts.how:
1. Get the slides or handout before the class (PDF on a tablet, or printed).
  2. During the class, write only what is not on the slide: the reason, the example, the link to an earlier topic, the lecturer's hints about the exam.
  3. After the class, add a question in the margin of each important slide.
  4. Mark slides you do not understand with a symbol and fix them within a few days.

examples.simple: A statistics slide gives the formula for standard deviation. You write next to it: "why divide by n-1? Because the sample mean is closer to the data than the true mean, so we would underestimate spread."
examples.nontrivial: A first-year law lecture uses slides that list case names and holdings. Rather than copy the holdings, you annotate each case with a one-line fact pattern and an arrow to the case it distinguishes or overrules. The slides now show the line of reasoning between cases, which is what problem questions test and what the bare list could not show.
examples.html:

  • Non-trivial: A first-year law lecture uses slides that list case names and holdings. Rather than copy the holdings, you annotate each case with a one-line fact pattern and an arrow to the case it distinguishes or overrules. The slides now show the line of reasoning between cases, which is what problem questions test and what the bare list could not show.

parts.time: About the cost of highlighting (~1-1.5 min per paragraph-sized slide, ~2-3×), plus about one recall question's worth (~30 s, 1×) for each "why" you add. Rewriting the slide content by hand costs several times more and adds little.
parts.watch: Annotating can drift into colourful highlighting of what is already there. If an annotation does not add a reason, an example or a question, it is decoration.

items.title: Concept maps
items.leadHtml: Boxes and labelled arrows (causes, inhibits, leads to, is an example of) show how ideas connect. Redraw them from memory a few days later.

parts.why: Linear notes store ideas in the order you met them; a concept map stores them in the order they relate. The labels on the arrows are where the learning happens, because writing "raises", "requires" or "contradicts" forces you to state the relationship rather than just place two ideas near each other. Redrawing the map from memory adds retrieval: in one well-known experiment, students who practised recall learned more than students who built concept maps with the text open, and later work found that building the map from memory works about as well as written recall.
parts.how:
1. List the 8-15 key ideas of a topic.
  2. Put the most general idea in the middle or at the top.
  3. Connect ideas with arrows, and write a verb or short phrase on every arrow.
  4. Look for cross-links between distant parts of the map; these are often the insights.
  5. A few days later, redraw it on a blank page without looking, then compare and fix it in another colour.

examples.simple: An ecology map: "sunlight → (powers) → plants → (eaten by) → herbivores → (eaten by) → predators", with "decomposers → (return nutrients to) → soil → (feeds) → plants" closing the loop.
examples.nontrivial: A map of the 2008 financial crisis for an economics or history course. Drawing it reveals a feedback loop (falling house prices → mortgage defaults → bank losses → less lending → falling house prices) that a linear list of causes hides. Finding the loop yourself is the moment you understand why the crisis spread.

items.title: Flowcharts and pathway sketches
items.leadHtml: For anything that unfolds as a chain of steps or of cause and effect, draw the chain: a historical sequence of causes, an algorithm, a legal procedure, a chemical or metabolic pathway, the course of a disease, a supply-and-demand shock.

parts.why: Processes are hard to hold in words because each step depends on the one before. A sketch lets you see the whole chain at once and spot where a branch, a loop or a missing step is. Drawing also gives the memory two routes in, a verbal one and a visual one (dual coding). And a sketch is easy to test: cover one box and ask what goes there, or ask "what happens downstream if this step fails?"
parts.how:
1. Write the start and the end of the process first.
  2. Fill in the steps between them as boxes, with arrows for "leads to".
  3. Mark decision points (diamonds or "if...then") and feedback loops.
  4. Add one short label per arrow explaining why one step leads to the next.
  5. Later, redraw it from memory, then predict what happens if you break one link.

examples.simple: A programming exercise: before coding a login form, sketch the flow "enter password → check against stored hash → match? → yes: open session / no: count attempts → 3 failures? → lock account".
examples.nontrivial: The path to the French Revolution drawn as a chain: war debts → fiscal crisis → Estates-General called → dispute over voting → Third Estate declares National Assembly → Bastille. Sketching it shows that the chain has a trigger (fiscal crisis) sitting on top of slower conditions (social inequality, Enlightenment ideas), and that the same trigger without those conditions might have produced only a reform. In biochemistry the same habit makes glycolysis or the Krebs cycle learnable: ask which step uses ATP, which produces it, and what happens to the whole pathway if one enzyme is blocked.

  • Non-trivial: The path to the French Revolution drawn as a chain: war debts → fiscal crisis → Estates-General called → dispute over voting → Third Estate declares National Assembly → Bastille. Sketching it shows that the chain has a trigger (fiscal crisis) sitting on top of slower conditions (social inequality, Enlightenment ideas), and that the same trigger without those conditions might have produced only a reform. parts.watch: Spending your time on neat shapes and colours instead of the arrow labels. A messy sketch you can redraw from memory beats a beautiful one you cannot.

items.title: Comparison tables
items.leadHtml: For things that are easy to confuse, make a table of distinguishing features: types of anaemia, antibiotic classes, verb tenses, rival economic theories, sorting algorithms, painters of one period, similar legal offences.

parts.why: Confusable things are rarely forgotten one by one; they get mixed up with each other. Studying them separately never forces you to notice the difference. A table puts them side by side on the same features, so your attention goes exactly to what tells them apart. Research on comparing cases finds a reliable benefit from comparison over studying cases one at a time.
parts.how:
1. Put the confusable items as columns (3-6 is a good size).
  2. Choose rows that discriminate: the features you would use to tell them apart in an exam question.
  3. Fill in the table, then highlight the one feature in each row that is unique to one item.
  4. To review, cover one column and reconstruct it, or cover the column headings and identify the item from its features.

examples.simple: Spanish past tenses: preterite vs imperfect, with rows "completed or ongoing?", "signal words", "typical use", "example sentence".
examples.nontrivial: Sorting algorithms in a computer science course: bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort, heap sort, with rows "average time", "worst case", "extra memory", "stable?", "when to choose it". The non-obvious insight comes from the rows, not the columns: quicksort is usually fastest in practice yet has the worst worst-case, so the table shows you why "it depends" is the right answer and what it depends on. In medicine the same layout separates types of anaemia by cell size, iron studies and typical cause.
examples.html:
• Simple: Spanish past tenses: preterite vs imperfect, with rows "completed or ongoing?", "signal words", "typical use", "example sentence".
  • Non-trivial: Sorting algorithms in a computer science course: bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort, heap sort, with rows "average time", "worst case", "extra memory", "stable?", "when to choose it". The non-obvious insight comes from the rows, not the columns: quicksort is usually fastest in practice yet has the worst worst-case, so the table shows you why "it depends" is the right answer and what it depends on. In medicine the same layout separates types of anaemia by cell size, iron studies and typical cause.

parts.time: About 10-20 min per table (~20-40×), but one table usually covers several paragraphs or a whole chapter.
parts.watch: Rows that list everything rather than what discriminates make a long table you will not review. Comparing similarities matters too, so add a row for what the items share.

items.title: One-page summaries
items.leadHtml: At the end of a topic, condense it onto one page. The act of choosing what matters is itself learning.

parts.why: A page limit is a forcing function. You cannot keep everything, so you have to rank ideas, merge details under principles and decide what the topic is really about. That ranking is understanding. But be honest about the evidence: summarising, as students usually do it (shortening the text while looking at it), was rated a low-utility technique in a major review. The benefit comes from making the summary from memory and from the decisions about what to leave out, not from producing a neat page.
parts.how:
1. Close the book and notes.
  2. On one page, write the topic's 3-5 main ideas and how they connect (a mini-map or table is fine).
  3. Only then open your notes, and add what you missed in a different colour. The added parts are your weak spots.
  4. Use the page later for blank-page recall: try to reproduce it before looking.

examples.simple: One page on the water cycle: four processes, one diagram, one sentence on what drives it (energy from the sun).
examples.nontrivial: One page on a whole term of introductory microeconomics. The page limit forces you to notice that most chapters are applications of the same two or three ideas (marginal thinking, supply and demand, incentives), so the summary becomes a structure rather than a list. For a long literature course, the same exercise might be one page per theme across several novels rather than one per book.
examples.html:
• Simple: One page on the water cycle: four processes, one diagram, one sentence on what drives it (energy from the sun).
  • Non-trivial: One page on a whole term of introductory microeconomics. items.bodyHtml:
At the end of a topic, condense it onto one page. The act of choosing what matters is itself learning.

Why it works. A page limit is a forcing function. You cannot keep everything, so you have to rank ideas, merge details under principles and decide what the topic is really about. That ranking is understanding. But be honest about the evidence: summarising, as students usually do it (shortening the text while looking at it), was rated a low-utility technique in a major review. The benefit comes from making the summary from memory and from the decisions about what to leave out, not from producing a neat page.

How to do it.

  1. Close the book and notes.
  2. On one page, write the topic's 3-5 main ideas and how they connect (a mini-map or table is fine).
  3. Only then open your notes, and add what you missed in a different colour. The added parts are your weak spots.
  4. Use the page later for blank-page recall: try to reproduce it before looking.

Examples.

  • Simple: One page on the water cycle: four processes, one diagram, one sentence on what drives it (energy from the sun).
  • Non-trivial: One page on a whole term of introductory microeconomics. The page limit forces you to notice that most chapters are applications of the same two or three ideas (marginal thinking, supply and demand, incentives), so the summary becomes a structure rather than a list. For a long literature course, the same exercise might be one page per theme across several novels rather than one per book.

⏱ Time cost. About 15-30 min per topic (~30-60×). Expensive, so keep it for the end of a topic or a revision checkpoint.

Watch out. Writing the summary with the book open turns it into copying. Pages that are too dense to recall from defeat the purpose.

items.title: Longhand vs laptop
items.leadHtml: Handwriting forces you to summarise rather than transcribe, which may help understanding. A tablet with a stylus works the same way. If you type, paraphrase instead of transcribing.

parts.why: The idea comes from a 2014 study in which students who took notes by hand did better on conceptual questions than students who typed; the typists wrote more words and copied more of the lecture verbatim. The explanation was intuitive: fast typing lets you transcribe without thinking, slow writing forces you to choose. But the evidence is mixed. A careful replication in 2019 did not find the conceptual advantage, and a large direct replication in 2021 found only small, non-significant differences. The most defensible conclusion is that the device matters less than what you do with it: processing and paraphrasing helps, verbatim transcription does not.
parts.how:
1. Choose the tool that suits the class: handwriting or a stylus for maths, diagrams and formulas; typing for fast, text-heavy content or when you need searchable notes.
  2. Whatever you use, write in your own words and in fragments, not full sentences copied from the speaker.
  3. If you type, switch off notifications and other tabs; the distraction cost of a laptop is well documented even where the handwriting effect is not.

examples.simple: In a physics lecture, handwritten notes make it easy to sketch force diagrams and write equations; typing them would be slow and clumsy.
examples.nontrivial: In a fast history or philosophy seminar, a student types, but with a rule: no sentence longer than ten words, and every third line is a "so what?" comment. The notes end up shorter than a typical laptop transcript and closer to what the handwriting studies say helps, which shows that the active ingredient is the processing, not the pen.

items.title: Pre-reading (priming)
items.leadHtml: Spend 10 to 15 minutes skimming headings, figures and learning objectives before a lecture, a class or a long reading. You will follow it better and know where the hard parts are.

parts.why: Arriving cold, you spend the first half of a lecture building a rough map of the topic, and details slide past before there is anywhere to put them. A quick skim builds the map in advance, like looking at a route before driving it. It works even better if you try to answer a few questions before the class: research on pretesting and prequestions shows that even failed attempts to answer improve later learning of the material, because they make you notice the answer when it comes.
parts.how:
1. Skim the headings, the figures and their captions, the summary and any objectives. Do not read in depth.
  2. Write 2-3 questions you expect the class to answer, or try the end-of-chapter questions and guess.
  3. Note the one part that looks hardest; that is where your attention should peak in class.
  4. After the class, check whether your questions were answered.

examples.simple: Before a chemistry lecture on acids and bases, you look at the slides' headings and try to answer "Why is a weak acid weak?" You get it wrong, and the lecturer's answer sticks because you were waiting for it.
examples.nontrivial: Before a seminar on a 40-page reading in sociology or political theory, you spend 15 minutes on the introduction, the conclusion and the first sentence of each section. Now you read the full text knowing the argument's destination, so you can tell which sections are the argument and which are evidence or digression. The same skim before a music theory class might be playing through the piece once while looking at the score.

items.title: Learning objectives as a checklist
items.leadHtml: Many courses publish what you are expected to learn: learning objectives per lecture, a syllabus, exam board specifications, course or module outcomes, or a certification's exam guide. Turn each one into a question and make sure you can answer it with the book closed.

parts.why: The objectives are the closest thing you have to a list of what the exam is written from. Read as statements ("Students will understand X"), they slide past; turned into questions, they become a self-test that covers the whole course with no gaps. A 2020 study found that learning objectives worked much better when students met them as pretest questions than as statements.
parts.how:
1. Copy the objectives or specification points into a list.
  2. Rewrite each one as a question, using its verb: "explain" becomes "why/how", "compare" becomes a table, "calculate" becomes a worked problem.
  3. Answer each from memory, then mark it green (solid), amber (shaky) or red (cannot answer).
  4. Revisit amber and red items first; recheck the whole list before the exam.

examples.simple: A school chemistry specification point, "describe the test for carbon dioxide", becomes "What is the test for CO2 and what result do you see?" Thirty seconds, done.
examples.nontrivial: A university statistics module outcome says "choose and justify an appropriate test for a given research design". Turning that into one question is not enough; the verb "choose and justify" means you need a set of mini-scenarios ("two groups, non-normal data, small n") and must name and defend the test for each. The objective tells you not just what to know but how you will be asked to use it. The same reading of verbs works for a language exam ("can describe past events" means producing past tenses, not reciting rules).

parts.watch: Ticking an objective because you recognise the words. Only a closed-book answer counts.

items.title: Don't over-polish notes
items.leadHtml: Beautiful, colour-coded notes can become a form of procrastination. Notes are only as good as how often you test yourself from them.

parts.why: Polishing feels like studying because it is effortful and produces something visible. But the effort goes into lettering, layout and colours, not into retrieving or connecting ideas. Learning research distinguishes passive activities (re-reading, copying, highlighting) from generative ones (explaining, mapping, testing yourself); copying neatly is near the passive end, however long it takes. It is like spending your gym hour arranging the weights.
parts.how:
1. Set a time limit for making notes (for example, no more than half the time you spend testing yourself from them).
  2. Use colour only when it carries meaning (red for "I got this wrong", a consistent colour for causes vs effects), not for decoration.
  3. Accept messy first drafts. If a page needs to be clean, make it clean in the second pass, from memory.
  4. Check your ratio each week: hours making notes vs hours answering questions from them.

examples.simple: A student spends 40 minutes rewriting a biology chapter in four colours. The same 40 minutes could have been about 80 recall questions on the chapter.
examples.nontrivial: A language learner keeps an elegant vocabulary notebook with calligraphy headings and drawings. It is pleasant, and that motivation is real, so the fix is not to ban it. The fix is to make the notebook testable: fold each page so the target-language column is hidden, and use it for self-tests on the bus. The beauty stays; the notebook now does work.

items.title: Which note format for which material?
items.leadHtml:
No single format is best. Match the format to the shape of the material: is it a set of questions, a web of relations, a sequence, a set of look-alikes, or a big picture?

Shape of the materialBest formatExamples from different fields
Facts and definitions you must recall on demandCornell or question-based notesVocabulary and grammar rules in a language course; dates and treaties in history; definitions in statistics; drug names in pharmacology
Ideas that influence each other (a web)Concept mapCauses of the 2008 crisis in economics; food webs in ecology; themes and characters in a novel; hormones and feedback in physiology
Steps in order, causes and effectsFlowchart or process sketchAn algorithm in programming; a civil or criminal procedure in law; the build-up to a revolution in history; a metabolic pathway in biochemistry; the stages of a chemical synthesis
Look-alikes that are easy to confuseComparison tableVerb tenses in Spanish or French; sorting algorithms in computer science; rival schools of thought in philosophy or economics; types of anaemia in medicine; similar offences in criminal law
A lecture that already has good slidesAnnotated slidesMost lecture-based university courses: physics, psychology, engineering, medicine
A whole topic before an examOne-page summary from memoryEnd of a unit in geography, a term of microeconomics, a module of organic chemistry, a period in art history
What the exam will askObjectives turned into questionsSchool exam specifications; university module outcomes; professional certification exam guides (IT, accounting, medical licensing)

A practical rule: use the cheap formats (question-based or Cornell notes, annotated slides) for every class, and save the expensive ones (maps, tables, one-page summaries) for the 10-20% of ideas the rest of the topic hangs on or the places where you keep getting confused. Whatever the format, the notes earn their time only when you close them and test yourself.
